ote.title: Events in an open format (OTE)
ote.description: Open Tech Events (OTE) is an initiative driven by Community Builders to publish each community's events in a shared, open format. It exists so event data is not locked inside closed platforms: with a single file, any directory, website or bot can read your agenda. If your community publishes one, this directory will show your upcoming events automatically.
ote.waysTitle: How to generate your OTE file
ote.way0: Register the community and its events on eventos.wiki: the easiest route, it generates the OTE file for you.
ote.way1: Use the ote-tools agent skills so an agent writes the spec for you.
ote.way2: Create the events by hand with the OTE web editor.
ote.way3: Start from ote-template, a repo with several tools already wired up.

web.title: Website URL
web.description: Add the community's main website or most stable landing page.
web.bullet0: Examples: own website, official page or persistent microsite.
web.bullet1: If you've already used it as the main URL, there's no need to repeat it here.

eventsUrl.description: Link to the platform where they post events or tickets.

linkAggregator.bullet1: Useful when the community centralizes its presence in a single aggregator.

mailingList.bullet1: Add it if email is a relevant channel for following activity or interacting with other members.

rss.description: RSS or Atom feed to follow the community's posts.

forum.title: Forum
forum.description: Discussion forum or wiki the community keeps open, if any.

status.title: How to choose the status
status.description: Use the status based on the community's recent activity.
status.bullet0: Active: there are people running the community and it has had recent activity.
status.bullet1: Inactive: for meetups, usually applies if there has been no activity for more than a year; for conferences, if it has exceeded its usual cadence.
status.bullet2: Unknown: use it if it's unclear.

communityType.title: How to choose the type
communityType.description: Choose the main type that best describes how the community operates.
communityType.techMeetup: Periodic meetups, usually in talk format and contained size.
communityType.conference: Typically annual event, larger and with several talks or tracks.
communityType.umbrellaOrg: Groups local communities under a common brand or structure.
communityType.hacklab: Maker community with physical space and shared resources.
communityType.collaborativeGroup: People who collaborate on projects, events, content or other common initiatives.
communityType.metaCommunity: Organization that groups people who run or represent other communities.
communityType.mutualAid: The priority is mutual support through forums, chats, lists or other channels.

eventFormat.title: How to choose the format
eventFormat.description: Think about how the community's main activity usually happens.
eventFormat.bullet0: In person: they have in-person meetups and usually don't livestream them.
eventFormat.bullet1: Online: their activity is mainly online.
eventFormat.bullet2: Hybrid: there are in-person meetups and they are usually also livestreamed.
eventFormat.bullet3: Unknown: if you don't have enough context.

location.title: How to indicate the location
location.description: Indicate the most useful geographic reference for understanding where the activity happens.
location.bullet0: Use city or main region in a format like `City, Country`, for example `Barcelona, Spain`.
location.bullet1: Use `Itinerant` when the community changes city or venue depending on the edition or event.
location.bullet2: If you're not sure what value to put, it's better to open an issue to discuss it first.

parentOrg.title: What is an umbrella organization?
parentOrg.description: An umbrella organization is an entity that groups several local communities under the same network or brand (e.g. GDG Spain, PyLadies, Codebar). If your community belongs to one of these networks, select it here. The vast majority of communities have no umbrella organization.

shortDescription.title: How to write the short description
shortDescription.description: Summarize in one sentence what makes this community special.
shortDescription.bullet0: Indicate the organizational form if you know it: collective (without legal entity), non-profit association, foundation, cooperative, company with community activity, user group, etc.
shortDescription.bullet1: Prioritize what it offers, its focus or value proposition.
shortDescription.bullet2: Avoid repeating only labels, technologies or target audience that you've already marked above.
shortDescription.bullet3: An ideal length is usually between 140 and 220 characters.

geographicScope.title: Geographic scope
geographicScope.description: Which territory the community serves. It does not have to match where its events happen: a community can meet in Madrid and support people across Spain.
geographicScope.bullet0: Local: the community targets one town or metropolitan area.
geographicScope.bullet1: Province-wide: it covers a whole province.
geographicScope.bullet2: Region-wide: it covers an autonomous community.
geographicScope.bullet3: Nationwide (Spain): it covers the whole country, even if events cluster in one city.
geographicScope.bullet4: International: the community operates beyond Spain.

chat.lead: Paste one of these into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity. Hit "Copy" straight away, or expand the block if you want to tweak it first.
chat.useTheSearch: For ordinary lookups — "Python communities in Valencia" — the search and filters on this site are faster and more reliable than asking an AI. These prompts are for what the directory cannot do yet: cross-referencing, spotting gaps, and finding opportunities.

tribe.label: Find my people
tribe.hint: asks about your profile, then recommends
tribe.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I want to find communities that fit me, not just my topic.

**Before recommending anything, ask me.** First look at what fields the dataset carries and at the topic and audience catalogues, then ask me the questions that genuinely help you narrow it down: which topics interest me, where I live and how far I can travel, whether I prefer in-person, online or either, what kind of community I am after (recurring meetup, conference, hacklab, mutual-aid group…), where I am in my career, which languages I speak, and anything else the dataset lets you cross-reference that would improve the recommendation. Keep it conversational, two rounds at most, and offer concrete options so I can answer easily.

Once you have my profile, recommend 5 to 8 communities ranked by fit. For each: name, city, why it fits me specifically, and its link. Then add 2 or 3 I did not ask for but that might surprise me, and say why.

Data rules:
- Only use communities whose "status" is "active".
- "tags" and "targetAudience" are catalogue ids. The catalogues exist in Spanish ({{tagsUrl}}, {{audienceUrl}}) and English ({{tagsEnUrl}}, {{audienceEnUrl}}): same ids, translated labels. Use whichever helps you match.
- If "matchesAllTags" is true the community is generalist and fits any topic even with an empty list; same for "matchesAllAudience" and profiles.
- "location" is where events happen; "geographicScope" is the territory served.
- Never suggest URLs listed in "archivedUrls".
- If a record has "humanValidated": false nobody has checked it: warn me before I rely on it.

speaker.label: Where to give a talk
speaker.hint: asks about your talk, then finds the fit
speaker.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I want to pitch a talk and I am looking for where it would land best.

**Before proposing anything, ask me.** Look at what the dataset and the catalogues contain, then ask what you need to get this right: what my talk is about and at what level, whether I have given it before or I am debuting it, which cities I can travel to or whether it is online only, whether I want a small meetup to road-test it or I am aiming straight at a conference, what language I give it in, and which audience I want to reach. Ask conversationally, with concrete options.

Then give me two separate lists:
1. **Recurring meetups** ("communityType": "tech-meetup"): they tend to look for speakers continuously and are a better place to debut.
2. **Conferences** ("communityType": "conference"): their call for papers usually opens once a year; tell me what you can infer from the dataset about when and where they run.

For each: name, city, why it fits my talk, its link, and where available its events feed ("urls.ote") or events platform ("urls.eventsUrl"). Finish with a plan: which ones you would start with, and in what order.

Data rules:
- Only use communities whose "status" is "active".
- "tags" and "targetAudience" are catalogue ids. The catalogues exist in Spanish ({{tagsUrl}}, {{audienceUrl}}) and English ({{tagsEnUrl}}, {{audienceEnUrl}}): same ids, translated labels. Use whichever helps you match.
- If "matchesAllTags" is true the community is generalist and fits any topic even with an empty list; same for "matchesAllAudience" and profiles.
- "location" is where events happen; "geographicScope" is the territory served.
- Never suggest URLs listed in "archivedUrls".
- If a record has "humanValidated": false nobody has checked it: warn me before I rely on it.

volunteer.label: Lend a hand
volunteer.hint: asks your time and area, suggests where
volunteer.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I would like to volunteer with tech communities and events.

**First, ask me.** Look at what the dataset holds and ask the useful questions: where I live and how far I travel, how much time I can give and how regularly, what I can do or would like to learn by doing (event-day logistics, communications, web, finding speakers, mentoring newcomers…), which topics interest me, and whether I would rather join a large or a small community.

Then give me two lists: communities likely to need **ongoing** help (meetups, hacklabs, mutual-aid groups) and events that usually need **one-off** volunteers on the day (conferences). For each: how to get in touch ("contactInfo" if present, otherwise the most suitable channel in "urls"), and why you think I would fit.

Finish by writing me a short introduction message I can adapt.

Data rules:
- Only use communities whose "status" is "active".
- "tags" and "targetAudience" are catalogue ids. The catalogues exist in Spanish ({{tagsUrl}}, {{audienceUrl}}) and English ({{tagsEnUrl}}, {{audienceEnUrl}}): same ids, translated labels. Use whichever helps you match.
- If "matchesAllTags" is true the community is generalist and fits any topic even with an empty list; same for "matchesAllAudience" and profiles.
- "location" is where events happen; "geographicScope" is the territory served.
- Never suggest URLs listed in "archivedUrls".
- If a record has "humanValidated": false nobody has checked it: warn me before I rely on it.

synergies.label: Synergies for my community
synergies.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I run a community and I am looking for collaboration opportunities.

**Before analysing anything, ask me.** First work out which community is mine (search the dataset by name and show me the record so I can confirm), then ask what you need: what kind of collaboration I am after (joint event, speaker exchange, promotion, sharing a venue), whether I want to stay in my city or reach others, what I am short of right now (attendees, speakers, hands, visibility), and whether I would consider absorbing or reviving a dormant community.

Then give me three lists:
1. Active communities worth doing something joint with: adjacent but not identical topic, compatible area or scope.
2. Communities on my topic in other cities, in case a speaker tour or a multi-venue event makes sense.
3. Communities with "status": "inactive" in my area or topic that might be revived. Tell me how long since they were reviewed ("lastReviewed") and what their channel was.

Data rules:
- Only use communities whose "status" is "active".
- "tags" and "targetAudience" are catalogue ids. The catalogues exist in Spanish ({{tagsUrl}}, {{audienceUrl}}) and English ({{tagsEnUrl}}, {{audienceEnUrl}}): same ids, translated labels. Use whichever helps you match.
- If "matchesAllTags" is true the community is generalist and fits any topic even with an empty list; same for "matchesAllAudience" and profiles.
- "location" is where events happen; "geographicScope" is the territory served.
- Never suggest URLs listed in "archivedUrls".
- If a record has "humanValidated": false nobody has checked it: warn me before I rely on it.

gaps.label: Gaps in the ecosystem
gaps.hint: which topics and areas are underserved
gaps.text:
Read {{indexUrl}}: it is the open-data index for the directory of Spanish tech communities. Follow it to whichever files you need.

I want an analysis of the ecosystem. If narrowing it helps — one region, one family of topics, one audience profile — ask me first where to focus; otherwise do the whole thing.

Give me:
- Active communities per province and per autonomous region.
- Over-represented topics, and topics with very few or no communities, using the tag catalogue categories.
- Underserved audiences, joining "targetAudience" against the audience catalogue.
- Concrete gaps: topic-and-area combinations where nothing exists and the local tech population suggests something should.
- Which part of the dataset is unreliable, using "humanValidated" and "lastReviewed".

Finish with the five communities that, if someone founded them tomorrow, would close the biggest gap. And tell me what you cannot be sure about from this data.

The catalogues exist in Spanish ({{tagsUrl}}, {{audienceUrl}}) and English ({{tagsEnUrl}}, {{audienceEnUrl}}): same ids, translated labels. Use whichever helps you match.

agents.lead: Building an agent, or using Claude Code, Cursor or similar? Paste these instructions into its context (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, system prompt or rules file). They tell it where the data lives and how to read it without getting it wrong.
agents.noMcp: No MCP server needed: the data is a set of public static files, so any agent with network access can read it directly.
agents.llms: machine-readable index of every file and how to interpret it.

agents.robots: crawling policy: every crawler, AI crawlers included, is welcome.
agents.instructionsHint: paste into CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or your system prompt

organizers.lead: More and more people look for communities by asking an AI. This is what makes yours show up well in those answers:
organizers.step1: Make sure you are in the directory and your record is current. If it is flagged as not reviewed by a human, review it: that field tells models how much to trust it.
organizers.step2: Fill in topics and target audience using the catalogue tags. They are what an AI uses to decide whether your community matches what someone asked for.
organizers.step3: Keep a working main URL and archive the channels you no longer attend. A dead link that looks alive sends people somewhere nobody answers.
organizers.step4: An Open Tech Events feed on your record puts your events in the directory, in aggregators and in front of any agent, and lets people subscribe without depending on whichever platform you use or on an algorithm. More reach, from the calendar you already keep.
organizers.note: None of this needs Git: the directory form opens the proposal for you and a person reviews it.
organizers.helpCopy: Questions about the events feed, the tags, the form or anything else in the directory: get in touch.

openData.footer: This dataset is maintained by volunteers and it is incomplete. If a community is missing or a field is wrong, fixing it is the most useful thing you can do.
